blocks.html: To understand whether this fault was excusable in the said de Rols, it must be presupposed that, as all other human actions are either voluntary or involuntary a, so crimes too are committed either voluntarily or not voluntarily b. Crimes voluntarily done are those which are executed with a deliberate purpose of committing them c, as to kill a man by lying in wait d2, to rape a woman, to steal, to bear false witness, and the like things, which are not committed without fraud and evil intention e: and after the execution they are unpardonable and irremissible as regards men f, even though he who has committed the act afterwards repents of it g. Otherwise, no one would ever be punished. For who is he that, to avoid death, corporal penalty, or ignominy, would not say, "I repent"? Those crimes also may be said to be committed voluntarily which are executed through some anger and sudden passion, as if I should kill him whom I find abusing my wife h, or who sets himself to kill me i.

notes.citation: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book I as printed; the division of actions into voluntary and involuntary is at III.1 (1109b30 ff.)
notes.original: Ariſtote au j. des Ethiq.

notes.citation: Digest 1.3.1–2 (De legibus senatusque consultis, l. 1 Papinian, l. 2 Marcian)
notes.original: l. j & ij. D. de legib.
notes.gloss: D. 1.3.1 defines law as, among other things, delictorum quae sponte vel ignorantia contrahuntur coercitio — "the restraint of offences committed voluntarily or by ignorance"; D. 1.3.2 gives Demosthenes' and Chrysippus' definitions.

notes.citation: Digest 48.19.11 (De poenis, l. Perspiciendum, Marcian — Respiciendum is the incipit as the medieval texts read it), § 2, the last paragraph
notes.original: l. reſpiciendum. P. final. D. de pœn.
notes.gloss: Delinquitur autem aut proposito aut impetu aut casu — offences are committed by design, by impulse, or by chance: Coras's whole threefold scheme in this annotation. The P. is the print's sort for §.

notes.citation: Liber Sextus, V.4 (De homicidio voluntario vel casuali), c. 1 (VI 5.4.1, Pro humani, Innocent IV at the First Council of Lyon, against those who procure killings by the Assassins; au vj. = in VI, the Sext)
notes.original: l. j. C. de homicid. au vj.
notes.gloss: The print's l. and C. are the civil-law sigla, but au vj. marks the Sext of Boniface VIII, whose title De homicidio is V.4; cf. the case file §6.2 on in VI.

notes.citation: Digest 48.5 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis coercendis), the penultimate law (fragment not identified)
notes.original: l. penultieme D. de adul.

notes.citation: Code 1.4 (De episcopali audientia), l. 3 (C. 1.4.3, the Easter amnesty, from which grave criminals are excluded); and Decretals X 5.12 (De homicidio voluntario vel casuali), c. 1 (X 5.12.1, Si quis per industriam occiderit proximum suum et per insidias, ab altari meo evelles eum, ut moriatur)
notes.original: l iij. c. de epiſ. au c. i. c. de homicid. aux Decretales.
notes.gloss: Aux Decretales marks the second citation as the Liber Extra; the first c. is the Code.

notes.citation: Digest 47.2.66 (De furtis, l. Qui ea mente, Maecianus; 47.2.65 in some editions); and Decretals X 2.1 (De iudiciis), c. Cum non ab homine (cf. X 2.1.10)
notes.original: l. qui ea mẽte. D. de fur. c cum non ab hom. de Iud.
notes.gloss: Qui ea mente alienum quid contrectavit ut lucrifaceret, tametsi mutato consilio id domino postea reddidit, fur est: nemo enim tali peccato paenitentia sua nocens esse desinit — "no one ceases to be guilty of such an offence by his repentance": Coras's point exactly.

notes.citation: Code 9.9.4 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis, l. Gracchus, Alexander Severus)
notes.original: l. Gracchus. C de adult.
notes.gloss: Gracchus, caught in adultery by night and killed by Numerius: the husband who kills the adulterer is not punished as a homicide if the man was of the condition the lex Iulia allowed to be killed.

notes.citation: Digest 1.1.3 (De iustitia et iure, l. Ut vim, Florentinus); and Gratian, Decretum, the last chapter of Distinctio 35 as printed — D. 35 ends with c. 9 (Ante omnia clericis vetetur ebrietas), on clerical drunkenness, which has nothing on self-defence; the number is probably a wrong sort; unidentified
notes.original: l. vt vim. D. de iuſt. & in c. final. xxxv. diſt.
notes.gloss: Ut vim atque iniuriam propulsemus… iure hoc evenit, ut quod quisque ob tutelam corporis sui fecerit, iure fecisse existimetur — what a man does in defence of his body he is held to do lawfully.

blocks.html: And this kind of fault, although at the execution there was some will, caused by this or a like passion, nevertheless, because such will was not premeditated nor deliberate, but rather forced and constrained by passion k, is easily pardoned l, especially since it is very difficult for a man so justly provoked to restrain and master himself m — witness him who dared to lay hand upon Pope John XIII and cut his throat, having found him misconducting himself with his wife n. Crimes not voluntarily committed are those which are excused as fortuitous, and by some disaster of error or ignorance o: as when Telegonus, son of Ulysses and of Circe, by chance killed his father, not knowing him, and thinking he had to do with the servants, who would not allow him entry into his father's house p. As likewise if, at the hunt, thinking to hurl the dart against a roe-deer, a boar, or other wild beast, one should meet with a man who died or was wounded by that blow q. And in the deed which here presents itself: if a woman, thinking she has to do with her husband, is known by another, or a man, believing he approaches his wife, converses with another, both are more worthy of excuse than of penalty r, as we shall discourse more amply hereafter. Otherwise Lot would have been incestuous when he got his two daughters with child, believing he had to do with his wife ſ. Certainly such kinds of offences, inasmuch as they proceed from no evil will, seem to be excusable t; unless there were some preceding evil work which had occasioned this deed u: for already he who committed the crime was in fault, exercising an act in itself evil and reprobate, whence his intention, considering the beginning, was corrupted and depraved. As for example: if I have the will to murder Antoine, and, thinking to slay him, I kill François, I am not excused: for my purpose has always been to kill a man x.

notes.citation: Digest 4.2 (Quod metus causa gestum erit), l. Si mulier (D. 4.2.21, Paul), the penultimate paragraph (D. 4.2.21.5, Si metu coactus adii hereditatem … quamvis si liberum esset noluissem, tamen coactus volui)
notes.original: l. ſi mulier P. penult. D. quod met. ca.

notes.citation: Digest 47.2 (De furtis), l. Verum (fragment not identified); and D. 1.1.3, l. Ut vim, cited at {i}
notes.original: l. verum. D. de fur. l. vt vĩ alleguee.

notes.citation: Digest 48.5.39 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis, l. Si adulterium cum incesto, Papinian; 48.5.38 in some editions), § Imperator (§ 8)
notes.original: l. ſi adulte rium. P. imp. D. de adult.
notes.gloss: The rescript of Marcus and Commodus: the husband who kills his wife taken in adultery, impetu tractus doloris, "carried away by the impulse of grief", does not suffer the full penalty of the lex Cornelia de sicariis, because it is most difficult to restrain a just grief (difficillimum est iustum dolorem temperare).

notes.citation: Platina (Bartolomeo Sacchi), Lives of the Popes (Liber de vita Christi ac omnium pontificum), the life of John XIII in Platina's count
notes.original: Platina en la vie des pa-pes.
notes.gloss: Platina's John XIII is the modern John XII (Octavian), said to have been struck down by the husband of a woman with whom he was taken in adultery, and to have died within days; Coras's luy couper la gorge sharpens the story.

notes.citation: Digest 48.19.11.2, l. Respiciendum (Perspiciendum), the penultimate paragraph as printed (the law has only §§ 1–2 in the modern division; the chance-killing is in § 2, cited at {c}); and D. 1.3.1–2, cited at {b}
notes.original: l. reſpicien dum P. penul. D. de pœn. l. j. & ij. D. de legib.
notes.gloss: Casu vero, cum in venando telum in feram missum hominem interfecit — "by chance, as when in hunting a weapon aimed at a beast kills a man".

notes.citation: Ovid, Fasti, book III as cited (3.92 names Telegonus as founder of Tusculum; the killing of Ulysses by his son Telegonus is told in the epic Telegony, in Hyginus, Fabulae 127, and alluded to in Ovid, Ibis 567–568 — the detail that Telegonus took his father for a servant is not in these)
notes.original: Ouide au iij des Faſtes.

notes.citation: Decretals X 5.12 (De homicidio voluntario vel casuali), c. Lator (X 5.12.9, on casual homicide not imputed to one without fault); and D. 48.19.11.2, the last paragraph of l. Respiciendum, cited at {c}
notes.original: c. lator. de homicid. P. final de la l. reſpiciẽdum. alleguee.

notes.citation: Gratian, Decretum, C. 31 q. 1 c. 1 (Leo: Nullus ducat in matrimonium quam prius polluit adulterio), read with Gratian's dictum after c. 2 — the woman who marries believing the union lawful adulterii aliquam habet veniam, dum eius copula creditur esse licita; and the chapters Si virgo and In lectum at "C. 33 q. 2" as printed — these two chapters, on the woman who lies with a man she takes for her husband, stand in the modern division at C. 34 qq. 1–2 cc. 5 and 6
notes.original: c. j xxxi q. j c. ſi virgo C. in lectũ. xxxiij. q. ij.
notes.gloss: The chapter Si virgo is cited again at annot-077 {a} for the rule that such a woman is not an adulteress until she knows.

notes.citation: Genesis 19 (19:30–38, Lot and his daughters); and Gratian, Decretum, C. 15 q. 1 c. 9 (Inebriaverunt)
notes.original: Geneſe c. xix. c. inebria uerũt xv q j.
notes.gloss: C. 15 q. 1 treats offences committed in drunkenness or madness; the chapter takes its incipit from Lot's daughters making their father drunk.

notes.citation: Digest 9.2.11 (Ad legem Aquiliam, l. Item Mela, Ulpian); and Decretals X 5.12.9 (c. Lator), cited at {q}
notes.original: l item Mel la. D. ad l. Aquil. c. lator allegué.
notes.gloss: Item Mela scribit, si, cum pila quidam luderent… — the ball that strikes the barber's hand so that he cuts the slave's throat: the classic case of liability without evil intent, where fault lies with whoever acted carelessly.

notes.citation: Digest 48.8.1 (Ad legem Corneliam de sicariis et veneficis, l. Lege Cornelia, Marcian), § 1; Digest 9.2 (Ad legem Aquiliam), at the paragraph Si fornicarius (D. 9.2.27.9, Ulpian, the only paragraph of the title so opening; the fragment's incipit is Si servus, which the print's l. q ſeruus garbles); and Decretals X 5.12, c. Continebatur (X 5.12.8, on casual homicide imputed to one engaged in an unlawful act)
notes.original: l. lege. P. j de ſiccar. l. q ſeruus. D. ſi fornicarius. D. ad l. Aqui. c. contine latur. de homi.
notes.gloss: The transcription's contine latur is Continebatur; l. q ſeruus is probably l. qui servus or l. quod servus, but no fragment of D. 9.2 with a paragraph Si fornicarius could be identified.

notes.citation: Digest 9.2.45 (Ad legem Aquiliam, l. Scientiam, Paul), § 4, the last paragraph; Digest 47.10 (De iniuriis et famosis libellis), l. Eum qui (the print's cũ qui), § Si iniuria (D. 47.10.18.3, Paul: Si iniuria mihi fiat ab eo, cui sim ignotus, aut si quis putet me Lucium Titium esse, cum sim Gaius Seius); and Bartolus (Bartole) on D. 48.19.11, l. Respiciendum, at the last paragraph
notes.original: l ſcientiam. P. final. D. ad l. Aquil. l. cũ qui. P. ſi iniu ria. D. de iniu riis. Bartole en la l. reſpiciendum. P. final.
notes.gloss: D. 9.2.45.4: si defendendi mei causa lapidem in adversarium misero, sed non eum, sed praetereuntem percussero, tenebor lege Aquilia — if, defending myself, I throw a stone at my adversary and hit a passer-by instead, I am liable: the stone meant for one man and striking another, which is Coras's Antoine and François.
